findings.source_passage: mistifying the gardens of the deep, as with so many sprinkling or mistifying pots
findings.why_it_matters: The 'mistifying pots' image is a characteristically Melvillean comic-grotesque domestication of the sublime; the draft strips the opening sentence to bare fact, losing the rhetorical extravagance that gives the paragraph its ironic voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'sprinkling and mistifying the gardens of the deep, as with so many sprinkling or mistifying pots' clause in the opening sentence.

findings.source_passage: Not so much thy skill, then, O hunter, as the great necessities that strike the victory to thee!
findings.why_it_matters: The apostrophe to the hunter ('O hunter') is rhetorically distinctive and interpretively important—it reframes the chase as necessity-driven rather than heroic; the draft paraphrases it into a flat declarative and drops the direct address.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the verbatim apostrophe: 'Not so much thy skill, then, O hunter, as the great necessities that strike the victory to thee!'

findings.source_passage: But why pester one with all this reasoning on the subject? Speak out! You have seen him spout; then declare what the spout is; can you not tell water from air? My dear sir, in this world it is not so easy to settle these plain things. I have ever found your plain things the knottiest of all.
findings.source_locator: penultimate paragraph before the 'central body' description
findings.why_it_matters: This is one of the segment's most voice-establishing digressions—the narrator's sudden mock-exasperated turn to the reader, with the paradox 'I have ever found your plain things the knottiest of all,' is a signature moment of Ishmael's rhetorical personality and is entirely absent from the draft.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert the full 'But why pester one' passage before the description of the central body of the spout; it is too distinctive to compress away.

findings.source_passage: No roses, no violets, no Cologne-water in the sea.
findings.source_locator: paragraph on the whale's sense of smell
findings.why_it_matters: The olfactory paragraph—including the comic punch-line about roses, violets, and Cologne-water—is entirely cut from the draft. The closing sentence is widely recognizable as a signature Melvillean comic aside and carries thematic weight (the whale's alien sensory world).
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at minimum the sentence 'But what does he want of them? No roses, no violets, no Cologne-water in the sea.' and brief context.

findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'incommunicable contemplations' is one of Melville's most resonant compounds in this chapter, linking the whale's mystical interiority to the rainbow/thought metaphor; the draft simply writes 'a canopy of vapor' without this phrase.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'engendered by his incommunicable contemplations' after 'canopy of vapor.'

summary: The draft achieves reasonable factual coverage but erases three significant voice-establishing passages—the mock-exasperated reader address ('But why pester one'), the olfactory comedy ('No roses, no violets'), and the rhetorically distinctive apostrophe to the hunter—producing three medium-severity findings that together require regeneration.
